newsitem.title: USA: Levi's launches "dream-logic" brand image campaign.
newsitem.headline: Levi's launches "dream-logic" brand image campaign.

text.p: Jean maker Levi Strauss & Co. on Wednesday unveiled an ambitious advertising campaign featuring television spots that it says aim squarely at the "originality and youthfulness" of the target 18- to 22-year-old consumer.
The commercials, which being Monday, are heavy on imagery light on use of the company name.
They were created by ad agency Foote Cone & Belding of San Francisco, a unit of True North Communications.
San Francisco-based Levi's, which holds the dominant position in the $8.7 billion jeans industry, is battling competition from designer jeans and private label brands.

Spending levels for the new campaign were not disclosed, but Levi's said the campaign was the largest in the brand's history. A published report estimated the campaign at $90 million, but marketing manager Brad Williams said that figure was too high. Levi Strauss spent $86 million to advertise the Levi's brand last year, according to Competitive Media Reporting, which tracks ad spending.
Each of the four spots previewed Wednesday for reporters showed men, women and children of various ages and races in story lines that cut abruptly from one to another.

In what the company described as a "dream-logic narrative approach," the commercials have no discernible beginning or ending but are linked in that the last scene in one spot becomes the first scene in another.
Although there are quick shots of Levis jeans throughout the spots, the name does not appear until the end, with the line "They Go On."
"These commercials celebrate the Levi's brand and its core values of originality and youthfulness," said Mark Hogan, Levi's consumer marketing director.
Three of the four television spots already produced are 60 seconds long. A fourth spot of 90 seconds is scheduled to be shown at some 2,000 movie theatres this weekend.
The print and outdoor advertising part of the campaign begins in October. Bound inserts will appear in such magazines as Sports Illustrated, Rolling Stone and others.
